items.followUp: A body of mass 5 kg moves at 12 m s⁻¹. Calculate its kinetic energy.

rubric.why: Checks the condition for translational equilibrium.
rubric.description: States that the resultant force is zero.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the net/resultant force on the body is zero.

rubric.why: Checks that the first condition is illustrated by a suitable example.
rubric.description: Gives an example of translational equilibrium.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a relevant example in which forces balance.

rubric.why: Checks the condition for rotational equilibrium.
rubric.description: States that the resultant torque (moment) is zero.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the net/resultant torque or moment is zero.

rubric.why: Checks that the second condition is illustrated by a suitable example.
rubric.description: Gives an example of rotational equilibrium.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a relevant example showing balanced moments or no turning effect.

modelAnswer: A body is in equilibrium when it has no acceleration; the conditions are translational equilibrium and rotational equilibrium.
Translational equilibrium: the resultant force acting on the body is zero, ΣF = 0.
Example: a book resting on a table has its weight balanced by the table’s upward force.
Rotational equilibrium: the resultant torque (moment) about any point is zero, Στ = 0.
Example: a balanced seesaw has equal clockwise and anticlockwise moments.

items.followUp: A body weighs 5.0 kN and moves at 15 m s⁻¹. Find its kinetic energy. Take g = 10 m s⁻².

rubric.why: Checks conversion of the given weight to SI units.
rubric.description: Writes the weight as 12,000 N.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct SI value of the weight.

rubric.why: Checks use of the weight to find mass.
rubric.description: Finds the car's mass using m = W/g.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for obtaining 1200 kg using g = 10 m s⁻².

rubric.why: Checks selection of the kinetic-energy formula.
rubric.description: Uses the kinetic-energy formula.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for writing KE = ½mv².

rubric.why: Checks correct substitution and calculation.
rubric.description: Substitutes the mass and speed and evaluates the expression.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correct substitution or the correct numerical result.

rubric.why: Checks that the final answer is given with an appropriate unit.
rubric.description: States the kinetic energy with its unit.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for 240,000 J (or an equivalent value) with a correct energy unit.

modelAnswer: Given: W = 12 kN = 12,000 N, v = 20 m s⁻¹, g = 10 m s⁻².
Formula: KE = ½mv².
Substitution: KE = ½ × 1,200 kg × (20 m s⁻¹)².

items.followUp: Define latent heat of fusion and latent heat of vaporization, and state what happens to temperature during each change of state.

rubric.why: Checks that the definition is for a unit mass of substance.
rubric.description: Identifies the unit mass involved in latent heat of fusion.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the definition concerns unit mass (or 1 kg).

rubric.why: Checks the change of state and temperature condition for fusion.
rubric.description: States that fusion changes a solid into a liquid at its melting point without a temperature change.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the solid-to-liquid change at the melting point with no temperature change.

rubric.why: Checks that the definition is for a unit mass of substance.
rubric.description: Identifies the unit mass involved in latent heat of vaporization.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the definition concerns unit mass (or 1 kg).

rubric.why: Checks the change of state and temperature condition for vaporization.
rubric.description: States that vaporization changes a liquid into a gas at its boiling point without a temperature change.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the liquid-to-gas change at the boiling point with no temperature change.

modelAnswer: Latent heat of fusion is the heat required to change unit mass of a solid into a liquid at its melting point without any change in temperature.
Latent heat of vaporization is the heat required to change unit mass of a liquid into a gas at its boiling point without any change in temperature.

items.followUp: A hydraulic press has a large piston of diameter 40 cm and a small piston of diameter 4 cm. What force must be applied to the small piston to lift a load of 12,000 N?

rubric.why: Checks conversion of both piston diameters to SI units.
rubric.description: Converts the piston diameters to metres.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correctly converting the given diameters to 0.30 m and 0.03 m.

rubric.why: Checks use of Pascal's principle for the hydraulic press.
rubric.description: Equates the pressure in the two pistons.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for using equal pressure or an equivalent hydraulic-press relation.

rubric.why: Checks the relationship between piston diameter and area.
rubric.description: Uses the squared diameter ratio to relate the piston areas.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for using the correct area ratio based on the diameters.

rubric.why: Checks correct substitution and calculation of the applied force.
rubric.description: Substitutes the load and diameter ratio and obtains the applied force.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correct substitution or calculation.

rubric.why: Checks that the final force is stated with a correct unit.
rubric.description: Gives the force required to lift the car.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for 200 N or an equivalent value with a correct force unit.

modelAnswer: Given: large-piston diameter D = 30 cm = 0.30 m; small-piston diameter d = 3 cm = 0.03 m; load F₂ = 20,000 N.
Formula: F₁/A₁ = F₂/A₂ (Pascal's principle).
Substitution: F₁ = 20,000 N × (0.03/0.30)² = 200 N.
Required force = 200 N.

rubric.why: Checks the subject matter of nuclear physics.
rubric.description: Defines nuclear physics as the study of atomic nuclei and their properties or reactions.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the study of nuclei, their properties, or nuclear reactions.

rubric.why: Checks the subject matter of plasma physics.
rubric.description: Defines plasma physics as the study of plasma and its properties.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying plasma (ionized gas) as its subject.

modelAnswer: Nuclear physics is the branch of physics that studies the properties and behaviour of atomic nuclei and nuclear reactions.
Plasma physics is the branch of physics that studies plasma, an ionized gas, and its properties.

items.followUp: What is the least count of a measuring instrument? State how the least count of vernier callipers is found.

rubric.why: Checks the meaning of least count.
rubric.description: Defines least count as the smallest measurement an instrument can measure accurately.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the smallest measurable value of the instrument.

rubric.why: Checks the vernier-callipers least-count relation.
rubric.description: States that least count is one main-scale division minus one vernier-scale division.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct relation.

modelAnswer: The least count of vernier callipers is the smallest length that can be measured accurately with them.
Least count = value of 1 main-scale division − value of 1 vernier-scale division.

items.followUp: What is zero error in vernier callipers, and how is it related to zero correction?

rubric.why: Checks that zero correction is applied to readings to address zero error.
rubric.description: Defines zero correction as the correction applied to an observed reading to remove zero error.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for linking the correction to removing zero error from a reading.

rubric.why: Checks the relationship between zero correction and zero error.
rubric.description: States that zero correction has equal magnitude and opposite sign to zero error.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct magnitude-and-sign relationship.

modelAnswer: Zero correction is the correction applied to an observed measurement to remove zero error.
It is equal in magnitude and opposite in sign to the zero error; zero correction = − zero error.

items.followUp: Define displacement and give one example showing an object's position relative to a reference point.

rubric.why: Checks the meaning of position.
rubric.description: Defines position as the location of an object.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying position as an object's location.

rubric.why: Checks that position is specified relative to a reference.
rubric.description: States that an object's position is described with respect to a reference point or surroundings.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for including a reference point or equivalent reference.

modelAnswer: Position is the location of an object with respect to a reference point or its surroundings.
For example, a car 5 m east of a tree has its position described relative to the tree.
